claims.text: High-entropy alloys have chemically disordered, multi-element compositions with significant variations in local atomic connectivity.
A GNN augmented with experimental thermal-conductivity data can predict low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than traditional effective-medium theories.
The GNN's improved accuracy would result from capturing complex local atomic disorder.
The proposed GNN would be trained on at least 100 alloy compositions with experimentally measured thermal conductivities.
The training measurements would cover temperatures from 300 K to 800 K.
Phonon transport dominates in the proposed moderate-to-high-temperature regime.
A diverse training set spanning the target compositional space is required.
A three-layer GNN can encode local atomic connectivity, bonding environments, disorder, and spatial correlations.
The GNN can learn correlations between local structure and phonon-scattering pathways.
Multi-element disorder affects phonon transport through changes in phonon scattering.
Augmenting the model with experimental data calibrates and refines its predictions.
Experimental-data augmentation overcomes limitations of purely theory-based predictive approaches.
The GNN will predict thermal conductivity values more than 20% lower than those predicted by conventional models for benchmark high-entropy alloys.
Traditional effective-medium theories and limited regression models do not fully represent the effects of complex disorder in high-entropy alloys.
The approach should be most effective between 300 K and 800 K when the training data are representative of the target compositions.
The approach may generalize poorly to materials without significant local disorder or to compositions outside the training distribution.
The model should reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20% relative to conventional effective-medium methods on held-out alloys.
The model's predicted trends should correlate with experimentally measured thermal-conductivity trends.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines improvement as a greater-than-20% reduction in the predicted thermal-conductivity value, whereas the falsification rule defines improvement as a 20% reduction in prediction error. Lower predicted conductivity is not equivalent to greater predictive accuracy.
